§0The road to
§0Bankrekka was never
§0kind to travellers. Old
§0"Aunt" Marrow kept
§0the lantern at the
§0ford - she said it was
§0for the ferryman,
§0though nobody had
§0seen a ferryman in
§0forty years...
§0Merchants called the
§0crossing "the Long
§0Water" and paid her in
§0salt.

§0In the winter of the
§0third age the river
§0froze solid, and the
§0caravans walked
§0straight across. It's
§0said that Marrow wept,
§0because the ice made
§0her lantern useless;
§0it's also said she
§0laughed. Both stories
§0survive in the tavern
§0songs - pick
§0whichever suits the
§0hour.

§0- Salt, iron and wool
§0came north.
§0- Glass, books and
§0rumour went south.

§0When the thaw came,
§0the lantern was gone.
§0Some say a pilgrim
§0took it to the shrine
§0at Ouroboros; others
§0swear it still burns
§0under the ice, waiting
§0for a ferryman who
§0will never row again.
